Day. "Beautiful, it is indeed beautiful, but it is not yet great." Yao asked: "Then how should it be?" Shun said:
<margin>Originally without contrived action to bring about governance, and the myriad things are naturally peaceful. Therefore</margin>
<margin>Sentence structure</margin>
Heaven’s Virtue brings forth peace. The sun and moon shine, and the four seasons proceed. It is like the sun and moon having
<margin>The appearance of movement and chaos</margin>
their cycles. The clouds move and the rain is bestowed. Yao said: "Then is it all stirred up and restless?" The Son
is the union of Heaven. I am the union of humanity. As for Heaven and Earth, they are what the ancients considered great,
and what the Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun collectively praised. Therefore, those of the past who ruled the world,
what did they do? They simply followed Heaven and Earth.
<margin>Wishing to hide his written works in the Zhou archives</margin>
Confucius went west to hide his books in the Zhou archives.

[Cap. XI.] Habitaverunt autem principes populi in Jerusalem : reliqua vero plebs misit sortem ut tollerent unam partem de decem qui habitaturi essent in Jerusalem civitate sancta, novem vero partes in civitatibus. Benedixit autem populus omnibus viris qui se sponte obtulerant ut habitarent in Jerusalem. Hi sunt itaque principes provinciæ, qui habitaverunt in Jerusalem, et in civitatibus Juda. Habitavit [Al. add. autem] unusquisque in possessione sua, in urbibus suis, Israel, sacerdotes, Levitæ, Nathinæi, et filii servorum Salomonis.

Et in Jerusalem habitaverunt de filiis Juda et de filiis Benjamin : de filiis Juda, Athaia filius Aziam, filii Zachariæ, filii Amariæ, filii Saphatiæ, filii Malaleel : de filiis Phares, filius Baruch, filius Colhoza, filius Azia, filius Adaia, filius Joiarib, filius Zachariæ, filius Silonitis; omnes hi filii Phares, qui habitaverunt in Jerusalem, quadringenti sexaginta octo viri fortes.

Hi sunt autem filii Benjamin; Sellum filius Mosollam, filius Joel, filius Phadaia, filius Colaia, filius Masia, filius Etheel, filius Isaia, et post eum Gebbai. Sellai ¹, nongenti viginti octo, et Joel filius Zechri præpositus eorum, et Judas filius Senua super civitatem secundus.

Et de sacerdotibus. Idaia filius Joarin, Jachin, Saria filius Helciæ, filius Mosollam, filius Sadoc, filius Moraioth, filius Ahitut [Al. Achitob] princeps domus Dei, et fratres eorum facientes opera templi, octingenti viginti duo.

Et Adaia filius Jeroam, filius Phelelia, filius Amsi, filius Zachariæ, filius Phesur, filius Melchiæ, et fratres ejus principes patrum : ducenti quadraginta duo. Et Amassai filius Azreel, filius Ahazi ², filius Mosollamoth, filius Emmer, et fratres eorum potentes nimis : centum viginti octo, et præpositus eorum Zabdiel filius potentium.

Et de Levitis Sebenia ³ filius Asub, filius Azaricam, filius Asabia, filius Boni, et Sabathai et Josabed, super [Al. add. omnia] opera quæ erant forinsecus in domo Dei, a principibus Levitarum,

Et Mathania filius Micha, filius Zebedei, filius Asaph, princeps ad laudandum et ad confitendum in oratione ⁴, et Becbecia secundus de fratribus ejus, et Abda filius Samua, filius Galal, filius Idithun, omnes Levitæ in civitate sancta ducenti octoginta, quatuor.

Et janitores, Accub, Temon, et fratres eorum, qui custodiebant ostia : centum septuaginta duo. Et reliqui ex Israel sacerdotes et Levitæ in universis civitatibus Juda, unusquisque in possessione sua ⁵.

Et Nathinæi, qui habitabant in Ophel, et Siaba, et Gaspha de Nathinæis. Et episcopus Levitarum in Jerusalem, Azzi filius Bani, filiis Asabiæ, filius Mathaniæ. filius Michæ. De filiis Asaph, cantores in ministerio domus Dei. Præceptum quippe regis super eos erat, et ordo in cantoribus per dies singulos :

<column-break/>

A et Phathalia filius Mesebel, de filiis Zera filii Juda in manu regis, juxta omne verbum populi, et in domibus per omnes regiones eorum.

De filiis Juda habitaverunt in Cariath-Arbe et in filiabus ejus : et in Dibon, et in filiabus ejus et in Cabseel, et in viculis ejus, et in Jesue, et in Mola-da, et in Bethphaleth, et in Asersual, et in Bersabee et in filiabus ejus, et in Siceleg, et in Mochona ⁶, et in filiabus ejus, et in Remmon, et in Saraa, et in Jerimuth, Zanoo, Odollam, et in villis earum, Lachis et regionibus ejus, et Azeca, et filiabus ejus. Et manserunt in Bersabee usque ad vallem Ennom.

Filii autem Benjamin, a Geba, Mechmas et Aia ⁷, et Beth-El, et filiabus ejus : Anathoth, Nob, Anania, Asor, Rama, Gethaim, Adid, Seboim, et Neballat, Lod, et Ono valle artificum. Et de Levitis portiones Judæ et Benjamin.

[Cap. XII.] Hi sunt autem sacerdotes et Levitæ, et qui ascenderunt cum Zorobabel filio Salathiel ⁸, et Josue : Sara, Jeremias, Ezra [Al. Esdras], Amaria, Melluch. Atus, Sechenias, Reum, Merimuth, Addo, Genthon. Abia, Miamin, Madia, Belga, Semeia, et Joiarib, Idaia, Sellum, Amoc, Helcia, Idaia. Isti principes sacerdotum, et fratres eorum, in diebus Josue.

Porro Levitæ, Jesua, Bennui, Cedmiel, Sarabia, Juda, Mathania, super hymnos ipsi et fratres eorum, et Becbecia atque Anni, et fratres eorum. unusquisque in officio suo. Jesue [Al. Josue] autem genuit Joiacim, et Joiacim genuit Eliasib, et Eliasib genuit Joiada, et Joiada genuit Jonathan ⁹, et Jonathan genuit Jeddoa.

In diebus autem Joiacim erant sacerdotes et principes familiarum. Saraiæ, Amaria ¹⁰. Jeremiæ. Anania. Ezræ, Mosollam, Amariæ, Johanan. Milicho, Jonathan. Sebeniæ. Joseph. Arem, Edna. Maraioth, Elei. Adaiæ, Zacharia. Genthon, Mosollam. Abiæ, Zecri, Miamin, et Moadiæ, Phelti. Belgæ, Sammua. Semaiæ, Jonathan. Joiarib, Mathanai. Jodaiæ [Al. Joiadæ], Azzi. Sellai, Belai. Amoc, Eber. Helciæ, Asebia. Idaiæ, Nathanael.

Levitæ in diebus Eliasib, et Joiada, et Johanan, et Jeddoa, scripti principes familiarum, et sacerdotes in regno Darii Persæ.

Filii Levi principes familiarum, scripti in libro Verborum Dierum, et usque ad dies Jonathan, filii Eliasib. Et principes Levitarum, Asebia, Serebia, et Jesue [Al. Josue] filius Cedmiel : et fratres eorum per vices suas, ut laudarent et confiterentur juxta præceptum David viri Dei, et observarent æque per ordinem ¹¹. Mathania, et Becbecia, Obedia Mosollam, Telmon, Accub, custodes portarum et vestibulorum ante portas.

Hi in diebus Joiacim [Al. Joacim] filii Josue, filii Josedec, et in diebus Neemiæ ducis, et Ezra sacerdotis scribæque.

[Chap. XI.] Now the princes of the people dwelt in Jerusalem: the rest of the common people cast lots that they might take one part out of ten who would dwell in Jerusalem the holy city, and nine parts in the other cities. And the people blessed all the men who offered themselves of their own will to dwell in Jerusalem. These are therefore the princes of the province, who dwelt in Jerusalem, and in the cities of Juda. Each one dwelt in his possession, in his cities, Israel, the priests, the Levites, the Nathinæi, and the sons of the servants of Solomon.

And in Jerusalem dwelt from the sons of Juda and from the sons of Benjamin: from the sons of Juda, Athaia son of Aziam, son of Zacharias, son of Amarias, son of Saphatia, son of Malaleel: from the sons of Phares, son of Baruch, son of Colhoza, son of Azia, son of Adaia, son of Joiarib, son of Zacharias, son of Silonitis; all these sons of Phares, who dwelt in Jerusalem, were four hundred sixty-eight valiant men.

And these are the sons of Benjamin; Sellum son of Mosollam, son of Joel, son of Phadaia, son of Colaia, son of Masia, son of Etheel, son of Isaia, and after him Gebbai. Sellai, nine hundred twenty-eight, and Joel son of Zechri their overseer, and Judas son of Senua over the city second in command.

And of the priests. Idaia son of Joarin, Jachin, Saria son of Helcia, son of Mosollam, son of Sadoc, son of Moraioth, son of Ahitut, prince of the house of God, and their brothers doing the work of the temple, eight hundred twenty-two.

And Adaia son of Jeroam, son of Phelelia, son of Amsi, son of Zacharias, son of Phesur, son of Melchia, and his brothers, princes of the fathers: two hundred forty-two. And Amassai son of Azreel, son of Ahazi, son of Mosollamoth, son of Emmer, and their brothers very mighty: one hundred twenty-eight, and their overseer Zabdiel son of the mighty ones.

And of the Levites, Sebenia son of Asub, son of Azaricam, son of Asabia, son of Boni, and Sabathai and Josabed, over the works that were outside in the house of God, from the princes of the Levites,

And Mathania son of Micha, son of Zebedei, son of Asaph, the prince to praise and to confess in prayer, and Becbecia the second of his brothers, and Abda son of Samua, son of Galal, son of Idithun, all the Levites in the holy city two hundred eighty-four.

And the porters, Accub, Temon, and their brothers, who kept the doors: one hundred seventy-two. And the rest of Israel, the priests and the Levites in all the cities of Juda, each one in his possession.

And the Nathinæi, who dwelt in Ophel, and Siaba, and Gaspha from the Nathinæi. And the overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem, Azzi son of Bani, son of Asabia, son of Mathania, son of Micha. From the sons of Asaph, the singers in the ministry of the house of God. For the command of the king was upon them, and the order in the singers for each day:

<column-break/>

A and Phathalia son of Mesebel, from the sons of Zera son of Juda, at the hand of the king, according to every word of the people, and in houses throughout all their regions.

From the sons of Juda they dwelt in Cariath-Arbe and in its daughters: and in Dibon, and in its daughters, and in Cabseel, and in its villages, and in Jesue, and in Molada, and in Bethphaleth, and in Asersual, and in Bersabee and in its daughters, and in Siceleg, and in Mochona, and in its daughters, and in Remmon, and in Saraa, and in Jerimuth, Zanoo, Odollam, and in their villages, Lachis and its regions, and Azeca, and its daughters. And they remained in Bersabee even to the valley of Ennom.

The sons of Benjamin, from Geba, Mechmas and Aia, and Beth-El, and its daughters: Anathoth, Nob, Anania, Asor, Rama, Gethaim, Adid, Seboim, and Neballat, Lod, and Ono the valley of craftsmen. And of the Levites, the portions of Juda and Benjamin.

[Chap. XII.] Now these are the priests and the Levites, and who went up with Zorobabel son of Salathiel, and Josue: Sara, Jeremias, Ezra, Amaria, Melluch, Atus, Sechenias, Reum, Merimuth, Addo, Genthon, Abia, Miamin, Madia, Belga, Semeia, and Joiarib, Idaia, Sellum, Amoc, Helcia, Idaia. These are the princes of the priests, and their brothers, in the days of Josue.

Furthermore the Levites, Jesua, Bennui, Cedmiel, Sarabia, Juda, Mathania, over the hymns, they and their brothers, and Becbecia and Anni, and their brothers, each one in his office. Now Jesue begot Joiacim, and Joiacim begot Eliasib, and Eliasib begot Joiada, and Joiada begot Jonathan, and Jonathan begot Jeddoa.

In the days of Joiacim there were priests and princes of the families. Saraias, Amarias, Jeremias, Anania, Ezra, Mosollam, Amarias, Johanan, Milicho, Jonathan, Sebenias, Joseph, Arem, Edna, Maraioth, Elei, Adaias, Zacharias, Genthon, Mosollam, Abias, Zecri, Miamin, and Moadias, Phelti, Belgas, Sammua, Semaias, Jonathan, Joiarib, Mathanai, Jodaias, Azzi, Sellai, Belai, Amoc, Eber, Helcias, Asebia, Idaias, Nathanael.

The Levites in the days of Eliasib, and Joiada, and Johanan, and Jeddoa, were written as princes of the families, and the priests in the reign of Darius the Persian.

The sons of Levi, the princes of the families, were written in the book of the Words of Days <note>i.e., the Book of Chronicles</note>, and even to the days of Jonathan, son of Eliasib. And the princes of the Levites, Asebia, Serebia, and Jesue son of Cedmiel: and their brothers by their turns, that they might praise and confess according to the command of David the man of God, and observe equally in order. Mathania, and Becbecia, Obedia, Mosollam, Telmon, Accub, keepers of the gates and of the vestibules before the gates.

These were in the days of Joiacim son of Josue, son of Josedec, and in the days of Neemias the leader, and Ezra the priest and scribe.

queste il verso come prima scritto l'hauea, cioè Benche mille penne, Ne sono stanche, e gia per ogni valle, che tanto era quanto se detto haueffe per tutto 'l mondo. La onde il diuino giuditio mutandolo, e lasciandolo poi, come si legge, venne a fuggire quella arroganza, che gli si haurebbe per auuentura potuto attribuire. Onde altroue, Po, ben puoi tu portartene la scorza.

I dico; che dal di, che 'l primo assalto
Mi diede amor, molt'anni eran passati;
Si ch'io cangiaua il giouenile affetto:
E d'intorno al mio cor pensier gelati
Fatto hauean quasi adamantino smalto,
Ch'allentar non lassaua il duro affetto:
Lagrima anchor non mi bagnaua il petto,
Ne rompea il sonno; e quel, che in me non era,
Mi pareua un miracolo in altrui.
Lasso che son? che fui?
La uita al fin, e 'l di loda la sera.
Che sentendo il crudel, di ch'io ragiono,
In fin allhor percoffa di suo strale
Non essermi passato oltra la gonna,
Prefe in sua scorta una possente donna;
Ver cui poco giamai mi ualse, o uale
Ingegno, o forza, o dimandar perdono.
Ei duo me trasformaro in quel, ch'io sono,
Facendomi d'huom uiuo un lauro uerde;
Che per fredda stagion foglia non perde.

<column-break/>

PROPOSTO & inuocato, viene hora a la narratione, e dice, che dal di che 'l primo assalto, intendendo quello ch'egli hebbe quando era di xv. xvi. anni, non perche fossi stato altre volte d'altra dona che di M.L. innamorato, percioche se noi bene ordinatamente vorremo; per i gradi de l'humana vita salendo; gli appetiti di ciascuna età considerando andare, chiaramente vedremo nun'altra cosa cotanto esser grata al picciolo bambino, quanto le poppe de la nutrice sua, poi vn pomo, vn fiore, vn uccelletto, e cosi a poco, a poco crescendo, appena puote esprimere ben le voci, e le parole, e segnar co anchor non ben fermo piede la terra, ch'ei altro non desidera che co suoi pari trastullarsi. Fatto poi piu grandicello, vn cane, vn cauallo, e simil cose desidera, e finalmente giunto a la età gli cominciano a piacere le donne. e questo è proprio quel primo assalto, che qui dice il Po. hauerli dato Amore, a cui mostra ch'egli faceffe resistenza fino al xxii. anno, nelquale vinto poi da l'estrema, e marauigliosa bellezza di M.L. di lei fieramente s'accefe, M Lti anni eran passati, Si ch'io cangiaua il giouenile affetto. Molti, che molti anni dica il Po. si marauigliano, come quelli che credono che foggiugnendo egli: Si ch'io cangiaua il giouenile affetto, cominciafle a diuenir vecchio; non s'accorgendo, che se fett'anni soli che i Troiani erano andati pel mondo errando, diede Virgilio questo aggiunto, Molti, dicendo, Multosque per annos Errabant acti fatis maria omnia circum, che maggiormente lo poteua dare il Petrarcha a ix. che da li xiii. al numero di xxii. ascendono, ne quali egli cominciaua a cangiare il giouenile affetto: cioè a metter peli in barba, come si suol.

the verse as he had written it before, that is "Although a thousand pens, are tired of it, and already through every valley," which was as much as if he had said throughout the world. Whence, by divine judgment changing it, and leaving it then, as one reads, he came to flee that arrogance, which by chance could have been attributed to him. "Which gain faith for the painful LIFE," that is, they bear witness to how much my miserable life and anxiety is, and coming to the invocation (which is so closed that it is scarcely perceived that it is invoked) he says, "And if here memory does not aid me, let the martyrs excuse it, and let a THOUGHT also excuse it," that is, an amorous one, which gives it anguish, in such a way that it makes every other thought of whatever other thing one might wish flee, and furthermore it makes it forget itself; holding the INSIDE of him, the soul, and he the HUSK, the body. Whence elsewhere: "Po, well may you carry away the husk."

I say; that from the day when the first assault
Love gave me, many years had passed;
So that I was changing my youthful affection:
And around my heart frozen thoughts
Had made an almost adamant enamel,
Which did not allow the hard affection to loosen:
A tear did not yet bathe my breast,
Nor did it break my sleep; and that, which was not in me,
Seemed to me a miracle in others.
Alas, what am I? What was I?
One praises the life at the end, and the day at the evening.
For the cruel one, of whom I speak, feeling
That until then, struck by his arrow,
It had not passed beyond my garment,
Took into his escort a powerful lady;
Toward whom never did much avail, or avails,
Wit, or force, or asking for pardon.
The two transformed me into what I am,
Making me of a living man a green laurel;
Which for the cold season does not lose its leaf.

<column-break/>

HAVING PROPOSED & invoked, he now comes to the narration, and says that from the day that the first assault occurred, intending that which he had when he was fifteen or sixteen years old—not because he had not been in love with other women before M. Laura, because if we want to order it well; rising through the degrees of human life; considering the appetites of each age, we will clearly see that nothing is as pleasing to a small baby as the breasts of its nurse, then an apple, a flower, a little bird, and thus growing little by little, he can scarcely express his voices and words well, and mark the earth with a not-yet-firm foot, before he desires nothing but to play with his peers. Made a little older, he desires a dog, a horse, and similar things, and finally, having arrived at the age, women begin to please him. And this is exactly that first assault, which he says here that Love gave him, to which he shows that he offered resistance until his twenty-second year, in which, conquered then by the extreme and marvelous beauty of M. Laura, he was fiercely inflamed for her. "Many years had passed, / So that I was changing my youthful affection." Many wonder that he says "many years," like those who believe that by adding: "So that I was changing my youthful affection," he began to become old; not noticing that if for only seven years the Trojans went wandering through the world, Virgil gave this addition, "Many," saying: *Multosque per annos / Errabant acti fatis maria omnia circum* <gloss>And for many years they wandered, driven by fates around all the seas</gloss>, Petrarch could have given it even more to nine, which from thirteen to the number of twenty-two ascend, in which he began to change his youthful affection: that is, to grow hairs on his beard, as is customary.

Omni prenitida compositis corpore forma:
Nomen Pelagius, formæ splendore decorus.
Consilio prudens, tota bonitate refulgens.
Qui vix transactis iam tunc puerilibus annis.
Attigit ætatis primos flores iuuenilis.
Cumque fat inimitem patri sciret fore regem:
Tali merentem blandis voce parentem.
Mi chare pater mea suscipe verba libenter.
Et que commoneo sensu bene pcipe prompto.
Calleo namque tuam senio decrescere vitam,
Viribus et propriis neruos penitus vacuos:
Nec te posse quidem leuis quid ferre laboris.
Ast ego sed validis dominabor quippe lacertis:
Ad tempusque potens dominis succubere duris.
Quapropter moneo: precibus blandisque rogabo:
Vt tregi natum me deponas tibi charum.
Donec sufficias precium persoluere totum.
Ne tua canicies vinclis intercidat artis.
Tsenior contra dicebat voce seuera.
Define tanta loqui dulcissime define fili.
Ne merore meos ducas in tartara canos.
Nonne salute tua pendet tantum mea vita,
Et sine te spaciu valeo pie viuere nullum.
Te decus omne meu, tu gloria magna parentu.
Es quoque subiecti nobis spes sola popelli.
Quapropter patria prestat me linquere charam.
Ecnon hyspania uinctu penetrare superbam.
Qua te grandeue vinclis spem tradere vitæ.
On tulit ergo patre Pelagius ista sequente.
Sed mulcet dictis mente chari genitoris.
Et cogit blandis quod suasit velle loquelis.
Consenfit precibus tandem genitor venerandus:
Tradidit et natum, semet redimedo misellum.
Tunc rex Pelagiu iussit perducere secum.
Et lætus rediit patria victorque reuisit.
Vllus pro meritis credat factu fore regis:
Hoc quod tam pulcra uincebat denique pompa.
Sed mage iudicio secreto iudicis æqui.
Vt populus tanto correptus rite flagello:
Fleret tocius proprii comissa reatus.
Vel que Pelagius christi pro lege necandus:
Forte locum peteret quo se morti dare posset.
Ecnon sanguineu pro christo fundere riuu.
Impendens anima domino bene morte piata.

translation:
<header>OF PELAGIUS.</header>

With every shape of his body composed in beauty,
By name Pelagius, decorated with the splendor of his form,
Prudent in counsel, shining in all goodness,
Who, having scarcely passed his childish years,
Reached the first flowers of his youthful age.
And when he knew the king to be an enemy to his father,
He addressed his deserving parent with such flattering voice:
My dear father, receive my words willingly,
And what I advise, take in well with ready sense.
I am aware that your life is decreasing with age,
And your nerves are deeply empty of their own strength,
And that you cannot indeed bear any of the light labor.
But I shall indeed rule with strong arms,
And for a time be able to submit to the harsh masters.
Wherefore I advise: I will ask with prayers and flatteries,
That you hand me, your dear son, over to the king,
Until you have enough to pay the full price,
Lest your gray hairs perish in the bonds of art.
The elder, on the contrary, spoke with a severe voice:
Cease to speak such things, cease, my sweetest son,
Lest you lead my gray hairs into the underworld with sorrow.
Does not my life depend so much on your safety,
And without you, I am able to live no space of time peacefully.
You are my whole honor, you are the great glory of your parents,
You are also the only hope of the people subject to us.
Wherefore it is better to leave me behind than the dear fatherland,
And also to penetrate proud Hispania in bonds,
Where I might trade your life, the hope of my age, for chains.
Pelagius did not take this, therefore, as his father followed,
But he soothes the mind of his dear parent with words,
And compels him with flattering speeches to want what he advised.
The venerable father finally consented to the prayers:
And handed over his son, redeeming himself, the miserable one.
Then the king ordered Pelagius to be led with him,
And he returned happy, and revisited his fatherland as a victor.
Let no one believe this happened for the merits of the king,
That which he conquered with such beautiful pomp,
But rather by the secret judgment of the just Judge,
So that the people, corrected rightly by such a lash,
Might weep for the committed guilt of all their own,
Or that Pelagius, to be killed for the law of Christ,
Might by chance seek the place where he could give himself to death,
And also shed the bloody stream for Christ,
Wasting his soul to the Lord, well-atoned by death.

Similitudo est vel Disiuncta vel Continua.

Similitudo Disiuncta est, quando termini quatuor reipsa distinguuntur, ut 1.Pet.1. Qua in re exultatis tristitia paululum nunc (si opus est) in variis tentationibus affecti, ut exploratio fidei vestræ multo pretiosior exploratione auri, quod perit, et tamen per ignem exploratur, comperiatur vobis esse laudi et gloriæ et honori cùm patefiet Iesus Christus. Hic quatuor sunt termini, ut aurum ad ignem, sic Fides ad afflictionem.

Continua similitudo est, quando termini tantum tres ponuntur, sed quorum unus nempe fecundus bis sumitur: ita scilicet ut quemadmodum se habet terminus primus ad secundum, sic se habeat secundus ad tertium, ut apud Ciceronem 3. de legibus. Videtisne magistratus hanc esse vim ut præsit, præscribat recta et utilia et coniuncta cum legibus? Vt enim Magistratibus leges: ita populo præfunt Magistratus. Hic termini sunt tres, Lex, Magistratus, Populus.

Proportio similium inter se est vel ἀνάπαλιν, id est, inuerse, vel ἐναλλάξ, id est, alterne. Proportio ἀνάπαλιν est quando inuertitur ordo aut προτάσεως aut ἀποδόσεως tantum, aut etiam terminorum. Hinc Regula argumentandi. translation:
Similarity is either Disjoint or Continuous.

Disjoint similarity occurs when four terms are distinguished in reality, as in 1 Peter 1: "In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while, if need be, you have been grieved by various trials, that the genuineness of your faith, being much more precious than gold that perishes, though it is tested by fire, may be found to praise, honor, and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ." Here there are four terms: as gold is to fire, so is faith to affliction.

Continuous similarity occurs when only three terms are placed, but one of them, namely the middle one, is taken twice: so that, as the first term is to the second, so the second is to the third, as in Cicero, *On the Laws*, Book 3: "Do you see that this is the power of a magistrate, to preside, to prescribe what is right and useful and in accordance with the laws? For as the laws are to the magistrates, so the magistrates are to the people." Here the terms are three: Law, Magistrate, People.

The proportion of similarities to one another is either <term>ἀνάπαλιν</term> <gloss>inversely</gloss>, or <term>ἐναλλάξ</term> <gloss>alternately</gloss>. The proportion <term>ἀνάπαλιν</term> <gloss>inverse</gloss> is when the order of either the <term>propositio</term> <gloss>major premise</gloss> or the <term>apodosis</term> <gloss>conclusion</gloss> is inverted, or even the terms themselves. Hence the rule of argumentation: If certain things are similar, they will be <term>ἀνάπαλιν</term> <gloss>inversely</gloss> similar; as, if as gold is to fire, so faith is to danger, then as faith is to danger, so is gold to fire.

The proportion <term>ἐναλλάξ</term> <gloss>alternate</gloss> is when the antecedent of a given similarity is compared to the antecedent, and the consequent to the consequent. Hence the rule of argumentation: If certain things are similar, they will be alternately similar; as, if as

<header>Reconstruction of the Ritual</header>

A reconstruction of the principal acts in this ritual may be made from the commentary, but it is perforce scanty and deficient by the very nature of our sources. The priests naturally choose only the salient features of the ritual for their explanations, and the acts whose meanings are explained are not chosen in the actual order of their occurrence. That is evident from the small fragment given above. Taking the large Aššur text as a basis of the sequence of the acts of the ritual, the following analysis may be made, but it only provides a defective substitute for the real ritual, which will undoubtedly be recovered in due time.

(1) Bêl is imprisoned in the lower world and the celebrants seek to bring him forth. A celebrant rides in haste to some kind of sepulchre (?). That means Nebo, who hastens to the lower world to comfort Bêl, held captive in the lower world. 1–8.

(2) Celebrants hasten in the streets crying, ‘Where is Bêl?’ and a priestess prays to the moon-god and the sun-god to restore Bêl to life. She goes to a gate, which represents Bêl’s sepulchre. She probably represents Bêl’s wife or his mother. 9–11.

(3) Watchmen stand at the gate of Bêl’s temple, who represent the guardsmen of Bêl’s sepulchre. 12.

(4) Celebrants lament, because Bêl was bound and slain, and because he descended into hell. 13–14.
